summary: Presents High Capacity Textual Conventions for MIB modules that need performance history based on 15 minute intervals. They extend the conventions in RFC 3593 to 64-bit resolution using the conventions in RFC 2856. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives network management modules a set of named data types for counting events in 15-minute intervals with 64-bit counters. A manager can read the count of the interval in progress, the counts of past intervals and a running total. The RFC warns that the management rulebook does not fully support these types, so reading software must not treat them as ordinary counters.

questions: high capacity textual conventions 15 minute intervals
what are textual conventions in a mib
why are performance history intervals 15 minutes
subtitle: 64-bit counter types for MIB modules that record performance history in 15-minute intervals.

tldr.problem: Telecommunications equipment keeps performance history in 15-minute intervals, and the 32-bit counters in RFC 3593 are too small for interfaces with high traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines seven textual conventions, which are named data types other MIB modules can reuse: three small integer types for bookkeeping, one threshold type, and three 64-bit counters for the current interval, a past interval and an aggregate total.
tldr.outcome: The RFC calls this a limited and short-term solution that may be deprecated once a long-term one is defined and deployed. SMIv2 does not fully support these types, so software that reads only the Counter64 tag may misread them.

today: RFC 3705 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself describes the conventions as a limited and short-term solution that may be deprecated once a long-term solution is defined and deployed.

sections.title: The Internet-Standard Management Framework
sections.content:
Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB), and they are generally read through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information (SMI).

This memo specifies a MIB module that complies with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is the list of values a device publishes so that management software can read them, and SNMP is the protocol used to read them. This RFC defines no values of its own. It defines named types that other MIB modules reuse.

sections.title: Two Ways to Keep Performance History
sections.content:
When a manager needs performance history about the equipment it manages, a MIB module can be built in more than one way. The agent can count events on a continuous basis, and the manager reads the counter whenever it wants and works out the history itself. Or the agent can allocate events to buckets, where each bucket represents an interval of time.

Telecommunications equipment often uses the bucket strategy, and the standard practice is for the agent to maintain history in 15-minute intervals. MIB modules that collect history on this basis already exist for the DS1/E1, DS3/E3, SONET/SDH, ADSL, HDSL2 and SHDSL interface types, and they share a common set of textual conventions from RFC 3593.

A need has arisen for 64-bit versions of those conventions, which this memo supplies.
sections.plainLanguage: Performance history can be kept in two ways. One is a single counter that never resets, which the manager reads and turns into history itself. The other is a counter that is reset every 15 minutes, with each finished count kept in a history table. Telecommunications equipment uses the second method, and this RFC gives it 64-bit counters.

sections.title: Why 64-Bit Counters and What SMIv2 Forbids
sections.content:
Ideally the high capacity conventions would be based on a Gauge64 or Unsigned64 data type, but no such types exist in SMIv2. The next best choice would be to base them on the CounterBasedGauge64 textual convention in RFC 2856, but that is not possible either, because SMIv2 allows only base types to be used when defining a textual convention.

The conventions in this memo are therefore based directly on the Counter64 type, which brings four limitations:

  • The MAX-ACCESS of objects defined with these conventions must be read-only, because the MAX-ACCESS of the underlying Counter64 type is read-only.
  • No sub-range can be specified in object definitions using these conventions, because sub-ranges are not allowed on Counter64 objects.
  • No DEFVAL clause can be specified, because DEFVALs are not allowed on Counter64 objects.
  • Objects defined with these conventions cannot be used in an INDEX clause, because no INDEX clause mapping is defined for objects of type Counter64.

Use of these conventions assumes that the agent supports 15-minute based history counters, that it can keep a history of 96 intervals of 15-minute performance data, that it may optionally support performance data that aggregates the history intervals, and that it keeps separate tables for the current interval, the history intervals and the total aggregates.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook for these modules, SMIv2, has no 64-bit plain number type, and it does not allow a named type to be built on another named type. So the authors used the 64-bit counter type and accepted four limits: the values can only be read, they cannot carry a range or a default value, and they cannot be used to label a table row. The agent must also keep 96 intervals of history in three separate tables.

sections.title: The Seven Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module HC-PerfHist-TC-MIB is registered as mib-2 107 and defines seven conventions.

Three small integer conventions do the bookkeeping. HCPerfValidIntervals (Integer32, 0..96) is the number of intervals for which data was collected; its value is 96 unless the measurement was restarted within the last 1440 minutes, in which case it is the number of complete 15-minute intervals for which the agent has at least some data. HCPerfInvalidIntervals (Integer32, 0..96) is the number of intervals for which no data is available, typically zero except in cases such as proxies. HCPerfTimeElapsed (Integer32, 0..86399) is the number of seconds since the current measurement period began; for 15-minute intervals the range is limited to 0..899.

HCPerfIntervalThreshold (Unsigned32, 0..900) defines a range of values that may be set in a fault threshold alarm control. Because the number of seconds in a 15-minute interval is at most 900, objects of this type may have a range of 0...900, where the value of 0 disables the alarm.

Three Counter64 conventions hold the counts. HCPerfCurrentCount is the gauge for the current 15-minute interval, HCPerfIntervalCount is the gauge for a previous 15-minute interval, and HCPerfTotalCount is the aggregate of previous valid intervals, where intervals with no valid data are not counted.
sections.plainLanguage: The module defines seven named types. Three count small whole numbers: how many 15-minute intervals hold data, how many hold no data, and how many seconds have passed in the current interval. One is an alarm threshold from 0 to 900. The last three are 64-bit counters: one for the interval in progress, one for a past interval and one for the total.

sections.title: How the Counts Roll Over
sections.content:
The value of an object with HCPerfCurrentCount syntax starts from zero and increases when the associated events occur, until the end of the 15-minute interval. At that time the value of the gauge is stored in the first 15-minute history interval and the gauge is restarted at zero. If the agent has no valid data for the current interval, the corresponding object instance is not available, and a retrieval request returns an error saying that the instance does not exist.

For the history intervals, let X be an object with HCPerfIntervalCount syntax, Y an object with HCPerfCurrentCount syntax and Z an object with HCPerfTotalCount syntax. In a system supporting a history of n intervals, with X(1) the most recent and X(n) the least recent, the following applies at the end of a 15-minute interval:

  • discard the value of X(n);
  • the value of X(i) becomes that of X(i-1), for n >= i > 1;
  • the value of X(1) becomes that of Y;
  • the value of Z, if supported, is adjusted.

All three counts are non-negative, may increase or decrease, and never exceed 2^64-1 (18446744073709551615 decimal) nor fall below 0. An object assumes its maximum value whenever the underlying count exceeds 2^64-1. If the underlying count later falls back below 2^64-1, for example after a retroactive adjustment caused by entering or exiting unavailable time, the value of the object falls too.

Each count convention carries a note. The convention is not strictly supported in SMIv2, because the always-increasing and counter-wrap semantics of the Counter64 base type are not preserved. Management applications that rely solely on the Counter64 ASN.1 tag to determine object semantics may mistakenly operate on these objects as they would for Counter64 objects.
sections.plainLanguage: When a 15-minute interval ends, its count moves into the most recent history slot, every older count moves one slot back, and the oldest one is dropped. The total, if the agent keeps one, is adjusted. A counter stops at its largest value instead of wrapping round to zero, and it can go down again if the agent corrects earlier data.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This module does not define any management objects. It defines a set of textual conventions that other MIB modules may use to define management objects. Meaningful security considerations can only be written in the MIB modules that define management objects, so the RFC states that this document has no impact on the security of the Internet.

The text also repeats, for each of the three counter conventions, that it represents a limited and short-term solution and may be deprecated as a long-term solution is defined and deployed to replace it.
sections.plainLanguage: The module defines no managed values of its own, so the RFC says it does not affect the security of the Internet. The risk sits with the software that reads these values: it must not assume they behave like ordinary 64-bit counters, because they do not.

items.label: HCPerfValidIntervals
items.desc: Intervals for which data was collected, 0..96.

items.label: HCPerfInvalidIntervals
items.desc: Intervals for which no data is available, 0..96.

items.label: HCPerfTimeElapsed
items.desc: Seconds since the current period began, 0..86399.

items.label: HCPerfIntervalThreshold
items.desc: Fault threshold alarm control, 0..900; 0 disables the alarm.

viz.caption: THE FOUR LIMITS THAT COME WITH BUILDING ON COUNTER64

items.title: Read-only
items.text: Objects defined with these conventions must have a read-only MAX-ACCESS.

items.title: No sub-range
items.text: Object definitions using these conventions cannot specify a range of values.

items.title: No default value
items.text: A DEFVAL clause is not allowed on objects of this type.

items.title: No index use
items.text: Objects of this type cannot be used in an INDEX clause to label a table row.
